title: Design Thinking in Social Innovation
description: “It’s not ‘us versus them’ or even ‘us on behalf of them.’ For a design thinker it has to be ‘us with them’” -Tim Brown“Human-centered design is a philosophy, not a precise set of methods, but one that assumes that innovation should start by getting close to users and observing their activities.” – Donald A. NormanDesign thinking creates value through systematic innovation. The objective of this course is to enable students to apply design thinking to create social value through systematic social innovation. To elaborate, this course introduces students to design thinking theories, methods and skills and their applications in the context of social innovation. Design thinking is an increasingly important concept needed for an effective implementation of ideas. It supports development of human-centric solutions, and uses a design-based mindset to provide practical solutions to complex problems. According to Soule, Malhota and Clavier, social innovation “is the process of developing and deploying effective solutions to challenging and often systemic social and environmental issues in support of social progress.” Social innovation focuses on the ideas and solutions that create social value, which can come from the nonprofit, private and public sectors. Modern social problems are enormously complex and this course will emphasize the interaction between different social science disciplines in the formulation of feasible and practical human-centric solutions that create social value.The course is modeled on the MIT Sloan Design Thinking program, which consists of 9 modules (see list of topics below). In this course, through interactive experiential learning, students will learn the key concepts and methods in design thinking and apply them to solve a current real life social problem. The ideas and insights gained in this course will be further applied in the other CU-FLASH minor courses.Group work is thoroughly emphasized and interaction of students from different majors is strongly encouraged. Students will work in groups and each group will be required to i) participate in group learning activities in classes, ii) perform exercises, and iii) do a final project on social innovation. A series of social innovation case studies and guest lectures from social innovators will be presented to students, reinforcing the practical aspects of this course. Students are strongly encouraged to interact with these practitioners.
outcome: Students will understand what innovation is and how it creates social values.    Students will master the basic design thinking skills.   Students will learn concrete methods in identifying and emphasizing with user needs   Students will learn to translate user needs into product/service specifications   Students will learn and apply group creativity skills to co-create multiple solutions to a social problem   Students will learn the skills to select ideas for prototyping   Students will learn to apply modular and integral product/service architectures to design the building blocks of a product/service   Students will learn to perform financial analysis of their project, understand a product life cycle and select a product/service development process to suit their project need.   Students will appreciate the value of interdisciplinary exchange and collaboration in social innovation
syllabus: 1. Introduction to Social Innovation  2. Understanding Design Thinking  3. Identifying User Needs4. Product and service specification5. Brainstorming6. Prototyping7. Product and Service Architecture8. Financial Analysis9. Product Development Processes
required_readings: (For reference only, subject to change.)  Tom Kelley and David Kelley (2013), Creative confidence: Unleashing the creative potential within us.(This book introduces basic concepts and applications of design thinking.) Tim Brown (2009). Change by design: How design thinking transforms organizations and inspires innovation.  (This book discusses how design thinking converts need into demand through a collaborative process.)

title: Managing Creativity and Group Dynamics in Innovation Teams
description: How to go from idea formation to implementation? What makes a winning innovation team?Modern organizational environments require creative solutions and the setting up of interdisciplinary innovation teams have become increasingly common. While the concepts and importance of interdisciplinary teamwork are well embraced, the additional practical considerations needed to foster a successful innovation team are relatively new and less well understood. This course focuses on two important aspects needed for an innovation team – the nurturing of individual and team creativity and management of group dynamics in innovation team. This course will cover the following topics: The nature of creativity (Creativity is not a gift; it is an extraordinary outcome of ordinary processes); Lack of creativity is a mental habit (Can over-learning kill creativity? Does too much education kill creativity? Novel conceptual combination could be magical cure of our uncreative mental habit); Characteristics of a creative mind (openness to experience, counterfactual thinking, use of paradoxical frames, and having the growth mindset); How to reward creativity; How does collective genius emerge in an organization; How did genius get inspired; Team diversity and team creativity; Team leadership; Transactive memory and coordination; and Challenges of interdisciplinary collaboration. This course is highly interactive and emphasizes on active learning. Students should expect to share ideas and listen to viewpoints offered by peers. Besides theories, each class will feature examples of modern social and business group management problems in a variety of organization settings that require innovative ideas. Through experiential group learning activities, students will appreciate the skills needed to improve team effectiveness with an aim of becoming effective, forward looking and positive contributing team members in an innovation team.
outcome: Understand the advantages of building an interdisciplinary innovation team   Understand when diversity will contribute to and when it will hurt individual and team creativity    Appreciate the major personal and contextual factors that affect creative performance of individual team members.   Understand the basic skills in leading and managing an interdisciplinary innovation team   Identify suitable strategies for enhancing creative performance of the self and an innovation team
syllabus: Demystify Creativity    Is Lack of Creativity a Mental Habit?    What Are the Characteristics of Creative Mind?    Should We Reward Creativity?    Collective Creativity?    How Did Genius Get Inspired?    Team Composition   Team Leadership   Communication and Coordination   Interdisciplinary Collaboration

title: Introduction to Art Tech Design and Interactivity
description: This introductory course investigates computer coding and variable-based methods within visual arts. Participants will adopt a design thinking approach toward translating ideas into prototypes using micro-processors and sensors for creative outcomes. Students will consider interactivity as the processing of data and gain greater understanding of how this translates into an expression of art and technology. They will be presented with both technical and theoretical frameworks for exploring artistic expression, compositional strategies, design culture, and artistic experience. This course will serve as foundation for future courses on creative communications, media, technology, and cultural studies.
outcome: Understand and modify computer code. Adopt AI tools and methods for problem solving and coding. Understand basic robotic control systems and microcontrollers. Develop Creative and Kinetic Graphic Outcomes Understand design methodologies and cultural phenomena. Understand how to document and present creative / design works.
syllabus: Introduction to Art and Technology Understanding Artistic Experience Developing Compositional Strategies Interactivity and Sensors Microprocessors and Robotics Computer Programming and Control Systems AI assisted Coding Prototyping Life Cycles Documenting and Presenting Design and Creative Works Understanding Design Culture

title: Social Innovation Around the World
description: This course adopts an applied, comparative, interdisciplinary, and experiential approach to understanding how social sciences are applied innovatively to address real problems in different cultural, political, and economic contexts. Rather than studying theories in the abstract, students examine how evidence‑based innovations are adapted on the ground by local organizations. The focus is on translation of theory to practice, contextual sensitivity, and comparative learning that sharpens judgment about what works, where, and why.This course is designed based on the following principles:• Global competence with local relevance: Students learn to read a problem through multiple cultural lenses, then apply those lessons back to Hong Kong, which will be a critical skill for social innovation. • Evidence‑to‑action mindset: By observing working innovations and talking with practitioners, students see how data, design, and community realities meet, improving their ability to evaluate and adapt solutions rather than copy‑and‑paste them.• Experiential learning: Unlike most courses that rely solely on case readings or simulations, this course brings students abroad for structured field study during which they can learn from local experts, visit local practitioners, and interview local people on social science topics. • Problem focus: Each cohort explores a single theme in one locale, then translates those insights into an interdisciplinary innovation tailored to Hong Kong. It bridges global learning with local action. • Professional readiness: The course strengthens field research skills (interviewing, observation, rapid synthesis) and communication. These competencies are highly valued by their future employers.• Ethical and contextual judgment: Exposure to diverse institutions and social norms builds cultural inclusion and sharper ethical reasoning about implementation trade‑offs.
outcome: Students who complete this course are expected to be able to1.    Compare and interpret how social science frameworks are applied across contexts by analyzing how different disciplines conceptualize and address the course theme in Hong Kong and the destination country, identifying similarities, differences, and underlying institutional or cultural assumptions.2.    Conduct structured field-based inquiry during the overseas study by engaging professionally with experts and practitioners, applying basic qualitative methods (e.g., systematic observation, interviewing, fieldnote documentation), and synthesizing first-hand evidence into coherent analytical insights.3.    Critically evaluate observed social innovations by assessing their problem definition, implementation design, empirical support, ethical considerations, and contextual constraints, and by explaining why they succeed or encounter limitations in specific environments.4.    Translate global learning into locally relevant proposals by identifying which elements of an innovation are transferable to Hong Kong, what contextual adaptations are necessary, and how interdisciplinary knowledge can inform feasible, evidence-based solutions.

title: AI for Social Science Research
requirements: For students in Doctor of Social Science Programme in Applied Social Science
description: The course is designed to equip students with foundational knowledge and practical insights into the role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in social science research, with a particular focus on applied social science research in frontier technology sectors, policy areas, and decision-making processes for leaders in the public, non-governmental, and private sectors. Course participants will learn and discuss applications, strengths, and limitations of generative AI in the social sciences, including public policy and management, social innovation, and sustainability for society.
outcome: By the end of this course, students will be able to understand and learn: Introduction to generative AI in social science research through a foundational understanding of generative AI technologies, with a focus on their application in social science research, including key concepts, trends, and methodologies that are crucial for integrating generative AI into social science research.  Critical analysis of trends, strengths, and limitations of using generative AI in social science research.  Research skills and ability to formulate research questions and design studies that incorporate generative AI, ensure methodological rigor, and address ethical considerations in AI research. Catalyst for Research Idea Generation to conceptualize and refine new or existing research ideas that leverage generative AI to address current questions in applied social sciences, with a particular focus on applied social science research in frontier technology sectors, policy areas, and decision-making processes.
syllabus: 1. Introduction: AI for social science research2. AI and Research design in social science research3. Research ethics in Using AI for social science research4. Use/Limitations of AI in Research plan, process & causation5. Use/Limitations of AI in Research questions & methods6. Use/Limitations of AI in Interviews & qualitative methods7. Use/Limitations of AI for Sampling and structural analysis8. Field Trip I: AI applications in the public/non-gov sectors9. Field Trip II: AI applications in the private sectors10. AI for Qualitative and quantitative data analysis11. Field Trip III: AI applications in applied social science research12. AI ethics for Publishing work13. Final presentation

title: Seminar (I): Computational Social Science
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Architecture, PhD Communication, MPhil-PhD Psychology, MPhil-PhD Geography and Resource Management, MPhil-PhD Social Welfare, and MPhil-PhD Sociology
description: This main objective of this course is to familiarize pre-candidacy students in the Computational Social Science (CSS) Concentration of any graduate division in the Faculty of Social Science with the field of computational social science. In each semester, the seminar will consist of a combination of lectures, student presentations, and project-based learning-by-doing activities. Learning will be organized around constantly updated individual/team projects. Each project will be an opportunity for all students in the course to expand their technical know-how and toolkits, deepen their appreciation of innovation and collaboration in social science empirical research, practice the development and completion of original research, and accumulate inspiration for one’s research agenda.
outcome: At the end of each course, students would gain: familiarity with latest advances in multi/inter/cross-disciplinary research on computational social science,  project-based practice of doing CSS research,  expanded technical know-how and toolkits,  enhanced appreciation of innovation and collaboration in social science empirical research,  improved academic presentation skills, and  the practice of original research.
syllabus: The topics and contents of the seminars will be constantly adjusted over time to avoid repetition and individually tailored for each student.
required_readings: To be decided by course teacher.
recommended_readings: To be decided by course teacher.
